00001| --- 00002| title: Designing view transitions 00003| description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 00004| nav_title: View transitions 00005| --- 00006| 00007| In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 00008| 00009| Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 00010| 00011| React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 00012| 00013| This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 00014| 00015| ## Example 00016| 00017| As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 00018| 00019| We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 00020| 00021| You can find the resources used in this example here: 00022| 00023| - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 00024| - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 00025| 00026| Before starting, enable view transitions in your Next.js config: 00027| 00028| ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 00029| import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 00030| 00031| const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 00032| experimental: { 00033| viewTransition: true, 00034| }, 00035| } 00036| 00037| export default nextConfig 00038| ``` 00039| 00040| App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 00041| 00042| > [!NOTE] 00043| > The View Transitions API is supported in all major browsers, though some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally, the transitions simply do not animate. 00044| 00045| Then import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 00046| 00047| ```tsx 00048| import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 00049| ``` 00050| 00051| `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 00052| 00053| ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 00054| 00055| The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 00056| 00057| In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 00058| 00059| Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 00060| 00061| ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 00062| import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 00063| import Image from 'next/image' 00064| import Link from 'next/link' 00065| 00066| function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 00067| return ( 00068|
00069| {photos.map((photo) => ( 00070| 00071| 00072| 00073| 00074| 00075| ))} 00076|
00077| ) 00078| } 00079| ``` 00080| 00081| ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 00082| import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 00083| import Image from 'next/image' 00084| 00085| async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 00086| const photo = await getPhoto(id) 00087| 00088| return ( 00089| 00090| 00091| 00092| ) 00093| } 00094| ``` 00095| 00096| The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 00097| 00098| If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 00099| 00100| #### Customizing the morph animation 00101| 00102| The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"`. This assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 00103| 00104| ```tsx 00105| 00106| 00107| 00108| ``` 00109| 00110| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00111| ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 00112| animation-duration: 400ms; 00113| } 00114| ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 00115| animation-name: via-blur; 00116| } 00117| @keyframes via-blur { 00118| 30% { 00119| filter: blur(3px); 00120| } 00121| } 00122| ``` 00123| 00124| The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 00125| 00126| ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 00127| 00128| The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 00129| 00130| Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 00131| 00132| In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Example

As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_.

We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions).

Build passes, typecheck clean. Summary of changes:

- **`next.config.ts`** — enabled `experimental.viewTransition`.
- **`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — wrapped each thumbnail in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`}>` and tagged the product link with `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.
- **`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — wrapped the hero in the same-name `<ViewTransition>`, wrapped the page in a `<ViewTransition>` mapping `nav-forward`/`nav-back` to directional animations, tagged the back link `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`, and wrapped the Suspense fallback in `exit="slide-down"` and the content in `enter="slide-up" default="none"`.
- **`app/page.tsx`** — wrapped the home content in the matching directional `<ViewTransition>` so the grid slides in on return navigation.
- **`app/globals.css`** — added `via-blur`, `fade`, `slide-y`, `slide` keyframes, pseudo-element rules for `.morph`/`.slide-up`/`.slide-down`/`.nav-forward`/`.nav-back`, and a `prefers-reduced-motion` block that zeroes all view-transition durations and delays.
